morning.text: Morning. Cold one today. Colder in here than out there, somehow.
There's a biscuit tin on your shelf that frosted the whole trolley. And a photograph of Mrs Lowe from Canal Row, which is odd, because she says she's never had her picture taken.

Some of the people who come to your window have gone on ahead, love. You'll know them: the glass goes cold.

Frost belongs to the frosted. Never give a cold thing to warm hands.

intro.text: Morning, love! Dora Finch, turf accountant. Some daft beggar's walked off with my {briefcase|case}.
Brown leather. Inside: {an egg-and-cress sandwich|sandwich} I was saving, and {my racing form, two horses circled|form}.
{D.F. in the lining|initials}. Dora Finch. Left it in the bar on Monday night, didn't I.

claims.text: A racing form with two horses circled

answers.text: Ninefold Lass and Late Train. Late Train came in at five to one, bless him.
Egg and cress. Don't tell me it's gone off.
D.F. My old dad's case, that was. Same initials.

notMine.text: That's not it, love. Brown leather briefcase. Smells of cress.

missing.text: Given to a nervous little man in a bow tie? Hugo Haversham?
That weasel owes me eleven pounds. Now he's got my sandwich as well.

cases.missingLedger: You handed Dora's briefcase to Hugo Haversham yesterday. It wasn't here for her.

verdicts.ledger: The sandwich, the racing form, and D.F. in the lining. Dora's case went home.

reply.text: Lovely! And the sandwich. Ta, love.
Here, if you ever fancy a flutter, Late Train's running again Saturday.

verdicts.ledger: Every detail matched Dora's story. It was hers.

reply.text: You what? It's got my initials in it!

verdicts.ledger: An egg sandwich is unpleasant, not uncanny. It should have gone home with Dora.

reply.text: Locking up my sandwich? You're a strange one.

intro.text: Hello. I'm sorry, this will sound silly. The porter said you have a {photograph of me|photo}.
Me and my Jack. {On Platform 9|where}. But Jack's been away eighteen months. He's not home until... well. Soon, they say.
I just want to see it. Please. I'd like to keep it, if it's mine.

claims.text: A photograph of her and her husband, Jack

answers.text: Twenty to ten. The 9.40. That's the train his letter said he'd be on.

notMine.text: No, that's not it. It's a photograph.

verdicts.ledger: It was Harriet's, but the developer's stamp said Thursday: tomorrow. It isn't lost yet, so it went in the Iron Drawer.

reply.text: ...Thursday. The 9.40. All right. I'll be there. I'll be there anyway.

verdicts.ledger: It was hers, but it came from tomorrow. Things from tomorrow aren't lost yet; they go in the Iron Drawer.

reply.text: Oh. Oh, look at him. He's smiling.
I'll go to the platform right now. Just in case.

verdicts.ledger: Right not to hand it over. But a photograph from tomorrow belongs in the Iron Drawer, not back on the shelf.

reply.text: I see. I'm sorry for wasting your time.

intro.text: Victor Crane, antiques. I'm here for my great-grandfather's effects. {A tin of letters|tin}.
{Lieutenant A. Penhallow, 1917, on the lid|lid}. {Letters to some woman called Mabel|letters}. Sentimental rubbish, but they'll fetch a price.
I have documentation. There, on your counter. All quite in order.

claims.text: Letters to a woman called Mabel

answers.text: Penhallow. My great-grandfather. It's all on the certificate.
Mabel something. Who cares? The postmarks alone are worth a fortune.

notMine.text: Don't be absurd. The tin. With the frost on it.

verdicts.ledger: Crane knew the name on the lid, and he had a certificate (the ink was still wet). But the tin was frosted, and Crane's hands were warm. Cold things go only to the cold.

reply.text: Refused? I'll be back. With a solicitor.

verdicts.ledger: The tin was frosted, and Victor Crane is very much alive. Cold things go only to the cold.

reply.text: Splendid. Mind the frost, it's quite... it's quite cold, isn't it.

verdicts.ledger: It wasn't from tomorrow. It belonged to someone cold, who was on his way. Refuse Crane, and wait.

reply.text: The safe? Are you quite mad?

intro.text: Excuse me, miss. I'm awful sorry to trouble you. I've lost {a ring|ring}.
{In a little velvet box|box}. I had it in my waistcoat pocket on {the 9.40, this morning|when}, and then I didn't.
I was going to ask a girl to marry me. She's waiting on the platform. She's always waiting on the platform.

notMine.text: No, miss. A ring. A little velvet box.

verdicts.ledger: There was no ring in the drawers. Not yet. A sepia young man in a 1921 suit said he'd come back.

reply.text: I'll come back tomorrow. I'm good at coming back.

intro.text: Good afternoon. Penhallow. Lieutenant. I believe you have {a tin of mine|tin}.
{Letters to my Mabel|letters}. I wrote her every week from France. I never posted the last few.
And {my harmonica|harmonica}. The lads used to make me play "Mabel's Waltz" until they couldn't stand it.

answers.text: Penhallow, 1917. My mother painted that. She was terribly proud.
Miss Mabel Hart. 14 Canal Row. I'd know that address with my eyes shut.
That's her. Dented at Arras. Still plays, near enough.

notMine.text: No. I'm sorry. The tin. With the letters.

missing.text: Sold? To my... to someone who says he's family.
Then I'll have to go on without them. Mabel never did get the last ones.

cases.missingLedger: The Lieutenant came for his letters, but they'd gone to Victor Crane.

verdicts.ledger: The window frosted when he spoke. Lt. Penhallow had gone on ahead, and the frosted tin was his. He'll post the last letters now.

reply.text: Thank you. I'll deliver them by hand.
She always said I'd be late for my own funeral. Turns out I was.

verdicts.ledger: The window frosted: he was cold, and the tin was cold. It was his.

reply.text: Ah. Of course. Orders are orders.

verdicts.ledger: Frost isn't tomorrow. The cold tin belonged with the cold soldier.

reply.text: Locked away? Like the last ones.

evening.text: Did you see that young fellow in the old-fashioned suit? Walked straight through the barrier. Didn't open it. Through it.
There's a draught from Platform 9 tonight that smells like 1921. Don't ask me how I know.

gazette.headline: LETTERS FROM 1917 ARRIVE AT CANAL ROW
gazette.body: Residents of 14 Canal Row were astonished this morning to find a bundle of letters on the doormat, dated 1917 and addressed to Miss Mabel Hart, who lived there until 1958. The envelopes were cold to the touch.

gazette.headline: WAR LETTERS FETCH RECORD PRICE
gazette.body: A tin of unposted letters from the Western Front was sold at auction yesterday by Mr Victor Crane of Ninefold Antiques. The tin, Mr Crane admitted, "would not stop frosting".

gazette.headline: MYSTERY YOUNG MAN SEEN ON PLATFORM 9
gazette.body: Several passengers report a young man in an old-fashioned suit and flat cap, asking after "the 9.40". Platform 9 has not seen a regular service since 1921.
